analysis.one_liner: Requires big banks' credit cards to work on competing payment networks so merchants can avoid high routing fees.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2026 with a bipartisan sponsor team and 8 cosponsors, then referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which has taken no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Federal Reserve to write rules so that credit cards issued by banks with more than $100 billion in assets cannot be locked to one payment network — or to the two biggest networks, Visa and Mastercard. That would let any store that takes credit cards choose which network processes each sale, opening the door to lower processing fees. It also stops card companies from penalizing merchants for their routing choices or tying security technology to one network, and directs the Fed and Treasury to publish a list of networks owned by foreign states or deemed national security risks.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants of every size — grocery stores, gas stations, restaurants, online sellers — gain the ability to route credit card sales over whichever network charges them the least, instead of the single network their customers' cards carry. If banks and networks compete for routing, some of the savings could reach shoppers through lower prices. Smaller payment networks gain access to a market currently closed to them. Community banks and credit unions under the $100 billion asset threshold are exempt and unaffected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants and payment networks outside Visa/Mastercard

how_it_helps.text: The Fed must write rules barring large card issuers (those with, together with affiliates, more than $100 billion in assets) from restricting a credit card's transactions to one network, or to only the two largest networks by share of U.S. credit cards, so merchants can pick a competing network for each sale.

Issuers and networks may not penalize a merchant — financially or otherwise — for routing a transaction over an eligible network, and may not require the exclusive use of authentication or tokenization technology that other networks cannot process.

The Fed, consulting the Treasury Secretary, must create and regularly update a public list of payment card networks that are foreign-state owned or pose a national security risk, and transactions on the two largest networks are restricted if a network is on that list.
The rules reach card-present and card-not-present transactions alike, including website and mobile app payments, and take effect 180 days after the Fed issues final regulations.

analysis.who_pays: The payment networks that dominate credit routing — Visa and Mastercard above all — and the banks with over $100 billion in assets that issue most credit cards would lose routing exclusivity and the fee revenue that comes with it. Issuers warn they would make up the lost revenue by cutting card rewards or raising other fees on cardholders. Community banks and small issuers, and three-party systems like American Express and Discover, are exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Visa, Mastercard, and the largest card-issuing banks

drawbacks.text: The banks and networks that would lose fee revenue warn they would respond by cutting credit card rewards points, cash-back programs, or raising annual fees and interest rates on cardholders, so some of the cost could land on the very consumers the bill is meant to help.

Consumer savings are indirect: the bill reduces the fees merchants pay, and whether those savings show up as lower prices depends on competitive pressure in retail markets, not on anything in the bill itself.

The bill strips the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau of any authority to enforce the new requirements, leaving enforcement to the Federal Reserve and other banking regulators with no dedicated consumer-watchdog backstop.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a genuine bottleneck: Visa and Mastercard sit on both sides of nearly every credit card transaction, and merchants cannot shop for a better rate. Giving merchants routing choice is a real, structural fix, and the security-technology provisions try to address the main good-faith objection that rival networks are less safe. But the honest accounting is uneven: the direct winner is the merchant, the direct loser is the largest banks and networks, and the benefit to everyday cardholders runs through two uncertain steps — merchant pass-through of savings and issuer behavior on rewards and fees. Removing CFPB enforcement also weakens the bill's own rules. It is a pro-competition bill whose benefits to ordinary people are plausible but not guaranteed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2026 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Lance Gooden (R-TX) introduced the bill on January 13, 2026, joined by Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) as the lead Democratic cosponsor.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services.
The bill has 8 cosponsors, split evenly between 4 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
The action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action after the referral; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved the bill, and that favors the status quo: Visa and Mastercard keep their routing exclusivity and the largest banks keep the interchange fee revenue that the bill would put up for competition.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Visa, Mastercard, and the biggest card-issuing banks

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor team and the 8 cosponsors split evenly, 4 Republicans and 4 Democrats, and prior versions of this bill have drawn support from members of both parties; there is no record of roll-call opposition in this Congress.

industries.note: The two largest networks currently sit on nearly every general-purpose credit card and earn fees on each sale. The bill bars them from being the only — or even the two default — networks on large issuers' cards, forcing them to compete for routing. Their interest in keeping the current arrangement runs against merchants and, indirectly, shoppers paying higher prices.

Big banks collect interchange fees set largely by the network arrangements on their cards. Losing routing exclusivity puts that revenue at risk, and issuers have historically said they would offset it by cutting rewards or raising cardholder fees.

Every business that accepts credit cards would gain the ability to route sales over the cheapest eligible network, cutting processing costs that are currently fixed by the card's brand. Whether they pass savings to shoppers is up to retail competition, not the bill.

Networks outside the top two — including regional and newer entrants — gain access to a routing market they are currently shut out of, since cards could no longer be locked to the two largest networks.

Cards issued in a three-party model, where the issuer is the network or under common ownership with it, are expressly exempt from the mandate. That exemption spares Amex and Discover while Visa and Mastercard lose market power.

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions (assets under $100 billion)
industries.note: Issuers below the $100 billion asset threshold are exempt, so their routing and fee arrangements are untouched while their largest competitors lose exclusivity.

analysis.trajectory: Versions of this bill in recent Congresses attracted bipartisan sponsorship and a large merchant lobby but repeatedly died in committee without a floor vote. With the bill sitting in House Financial Services after months of inaction, the likely path is the same unless it is attached to a larger, must-pass bill.
